When scoping is enabled in this way, the provider captures the per-operation thread ID and uses it to enforce that only memories belonging to that specific operation’s thread are returned, changing correctness constraints to avoid “single-thread usage” violations under concurrency. In practice, this raises correctness expectations: concurrent/multi-threaded execution must not share the same scoped memory context across operations, because the provider will restrict grounding to the captured per-operation thread ID.

What does the WorkflowContext type parameterization enable handlers to do (e.g., sending messages vs yielding workflow outputs)?

The `WorkflowContext` type parameters declare what the handler is allowed to do: `WorkflowContext[T_Out]` enables sending messages of type `T_Out` via `ctx.send_message()`. If the handler uses `WorkflowContext[T_Out, T_W_Out]`, it can both `send_message()` messages of type `T_Out` and `yield_output()` workflow-level outputs of type `T_W_Out`. If a handler uses the unparameterized `WorkflowContext`, it is for side effects only (no sending or yielding outputs).
